newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - SOUTH AFRICAN BUDGET SUMS - BY E.OSBORN.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - SOUTH AFRICAN BUDGET SUMS - BY E.OSBORN.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

The extraordinary thing about the roadshow on February 20 put on by the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Reserve Bank was the spectacle of grown men floundering with the concept of the budget deficit.

There ws unedifying confusion among the economists putting questions to the Minister and the Minister, himself, seemed to be none too comfortable with the concept. The confusion lay with the relationship between the deficit, the borrowing requirement and the financing of that requirement.

Simplistically, the budget deficit before borrowing is the arithmetic excess of estimated expenditure over estimated revenue. In the 1996/97 budget, as presented last March, the projected deficit for the year was 28.8 billion rand, or 5.1 percent of GDP.

The borrowing requirement is then the sum of this deficit, as defined, and loan redemptions - in the 1996/97 budget 16.2 billion rand - giving a gross borrowing requirement of 45.1 billion rand. The Budget Review, tabled at the time of the budget, showed how the Ministry of Finance expected this borrowing requirement to be financed - in terms of short-term loans (3.0 billion rand), domestic loans (39.6 billion) and foreign loans (2.5 billion).

But in the Ministry of Finance's monthly release on the progress of the budget put out on February 4 it commented that because of an assessed six billion rand in respect of cash balances at the beginning of the year and surrenders the demands on the market would be reduced accordingly. This windfall was confused at the roadshow as a reduction in the deficit from 28.8 billion to 22.8 billion. This is not so, neither the totals of the deficit nor the borrowing, or more strictly, financing, requirement are changed. The only thing that does change is the amount that will be required from the market.

However, the Ministry had overlooked the fact that cash balances would have to be in hand at the end of the fiscal year for the immediate needs of the new fiscal year 1997/98. Government is an on-going business. The exit cash needs are probably of the same order as the entry cash balace of 3.3 billion in the Tax and Loan Accounts. There was a negligible nine billion rand in the Exchequer Account at the start of the year. The only windfall then is the amount of surrenders in respect of past year's issues. To the end of January these have amounted to 4.3 billion rand and this is the more appropriate figure for the reduced demands on the market.

But there is much more to this whole business than the simple equation between gross borrowing requirement and the deficit and loan redemptions. Clearly the financial markets are concerned with the gross borrowing requirements, and there is a preoccupation with the deficit because that is the major component of the amount to be financed. Everything is being preceived on a cash-flow basis without the complications of accruals. But on this cash-flow basis there are a number of debits and credits in the accounts that could affect the final amounts to be borrowed from the market and definitions and concepts should be extended to accommodate these.

On the credits or receipts side there are such things as capital revenues and surrenders. The capital revenues have in recent years primarily derived from the sale of strategic oil supplies but in the future could arise in quantity from the proceeds of privatisation not withheld for the purposes of reinvestment in the affected parastatals. The surrenders arise in respect of unspent issues to departments in earlier years surrendered back to the exchequer.

On the debits side there are the minor subscriptions to the IMF, World Bank and IDA, payments of guarantees and issues against the votes of previous years, described as "Late departmental requisitions".

In the past the Ministry has included capital revenues with ordinary revenues in the striking of the deficit simply in order to reduce the size of the deficit and its percentage of GDP - that is for window dressing purposes. The Minister has now given an undertaking that the privatisation proceeds from Telkom will not be taken into revenue and, therefore, the assessment of the deficit. The four percent deficit target is to be achieved on the basis of ordinary revenues and expenditure, which incidentally, include both recurrent and capital expenditures. He intends to use such proceeds into the exchequer for the reduction of debt. This being so these proceeds should be brought into the account in assessing the borrowing requirement from the market. Less will be required of the market.
Ideally, an estimate of surrenders during the course of the fiscal year should also be made before arriving at the financing requirements from the market.

Clearly the subscriptions to the world bodies are more appropriately included with the expenditure figures of the Ministry of Finance and will, therefore, affect the deficit calculation slightly. The guarantees, on the other hand, being contingent liabilities, should not be included in expenditures, but a provision should notionally be included in the assessment of the borrowing requirement.

The late departmental requisitions in respect of voted provisions in earlier years arise from the so-called roll-overs and these, too, should be estimated and provided for in the calculation of the borrowing requirement.

In the sum, the Ministry of Finance should put a little more effort into compiling a net borrowing requirement in its final Summary of the National Budget that appears at the end of the Budget Review, as follows:
National budget deficit (including world body subscriptions)
Plus: Late departmental issues
Guarantees
Loan redemptions
Less: Surrenders
Capital revenues (privatisation etc)
Imputed interest on zero-interest stocks
Net Borrowing Requirement.

The entry in respect of the imputed interest on zero-interest stocks allows for the fact that imputations are presently included in the interest bill, but as the whole budgetary process is on a cash-flow basis there has bo be a contra-entry with "other receipts" in the accounts. The same principle will have to apply once the Ministry has decided on an appropriate way of handling the amortisation of government stock, provisions for which may be included in the servicing of debt and therefore affecting the deficit. Similar complications could arise with any further move towards putting the accounts on an accrual basis. For the moment the accounts are on a cash-flow basis but for the relatively modest hybrid contamination of the imputed interest on zero-coupon stocks.

Finally there remains the question of the appropriate valuation of the foreign loans that are to be redeemed. At present the valuation is the original book value of the loans at the time of initial borrowing years ago. The forex loss on redemption is included with debt servicing costs and therefore adds to the deficit. Perhaps here it would be better to change the system and show the full estimated foreign redemption cost in the borrowing requirement; this would reduce the deficit. This would then bring foreign debt into line with domestic debt for redemptions of domestic debt are given at the full nominal value which, of course, is the cash-flow equivalent.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
